## Part A — Creating Data Frames

```{r}
# TODO: Create three vectors of equal length (5 students):
# name (character): "Ana", "Ben", "Cid", "Dex", "Eli"
# age (numeric): 20, 21, 19, 22, 20
# passed (logical): TRUE, TRUE, FALSE, TRUE, FALSE

name <- c("Ana", "Ben", "Cid", "Dex", "Eli")
age <- c(20, 21, 19, 22, 20)
passed <- c(TRUE, TRUE, FALSE, TRUE, FALSE)
```

```{r}
# TODO: Combine name, age, and passed into a data frame called students
# using data.frame(name = name, age = age, passed = passed)
# Print students

students <- data.frame(name = name, age = age, passed = passed)

print(students)
```

```{r}
# TODO: Check the type of the "name" column using typeof(students$name)
# and class(students$name)

typeof(students$name)

class(students$name)
```

```{r}
# TODO: Now create a SECOND data frame called courses directly, without
# separate vectors first, using data.frame() with these columns:
# course_code = c("IS101", "IS102", "IS103")
# units = c(3, 3, 2)
# instructor = c("Dr. P. Reyes", "Dr. R. Santos", "Dr. S. Cruz")

courses <- data.frame(
  course_code = c("IS101", "IS102", "IS103"),
  units = c(3, 3, 3),
  instructor = c("Dr. P. Reyes", "Dr. R. Santos", "Dr. S. Cruz")
)

print(courses)
```
Question #1: You created students two different ways in concept: first from separate vectors, then courses directly inline. Both approaches produce the same kind of object.

In your own words, explain why data.frame() requires every column argument to have the same length, and what error you would expect if they didn’t.

Answer: A data frame is structured as a rectangular table where every column represents a variable and every row represents an observation. If columns had different lengths, the table would have uneven rows, breaking the uniform grid required for tabular data analysis.

If you give vectors of unequal lengths that are not multiples of one another, R throws an error: arguments imply differing number of rows.

Question #2: A data frame is often described as “a list of vectors of equal length.”

Based on what you know about lists from a previous lab, explain why this description makes sense — specifically, why can each column hold a different data type while a single column cannot?

Answer: In my understanding, a data frame is implemented as a specialized list where each element of the list corresponds to a column vector. Because a list can hold items of different data types, each individual column can maintain its own distinct data type. However, because each column is itself an atomic vector, all element within that single column must share the exact same data type.

## Part B — Subsetting Data Frames

```{r}
# TODO: Access the "age" column of students three different ways:
# students$age
# students[["age"]]
# students["age"]  -- note: compare the output/class of this one to the others

students$age
students[["age"]]
students["age"]
```

```{r}
# TODO: Access the entire 2nd row of students using students[2, ]

students[2, ]
```
```{r}
# TODO: Access the value in row 3, column "name" using students[3, "name"]

students[3, "name"]
```
```{r}
# TODO: Return only the rows of students where passed is TRUE
# Hint: students[students$passed == TRUE, ]

students[students$passed == TRUE, ]
```

```{r}
# TODO: Return only the rows of students where passed is TRUE AND
# age is greater than 19. Use the & operator to combine both conditions.

students[students$passed == TRUE & students$age > 19, ]
```

Question #3

students["age"] and students$age both seem to give you the age column, but class() reveals they are different types of objects.

Answer: class(students$age) (and students[["age"]]) returns "numeric", whereas class(students["age"]) returns "data.frame".

Run class() on each and explain the difference, connecting it to what you learned about single vs. double brackets on lists in a previous lab.

Answer: This shows us that the single brackets ([ ]) extract a sub-list (preserving the data frame structure as a single-column table), while double brackets ([[ ]]) or the dollar sign ($) extract the underlying vector itself, stripping away the outer data frame container.

Question #4: In df-multiple-conditions, explain what the & operator is doing to the two logical vectors (students$passed == TRUE and students$age > 19) before that combined result is used to filter rows.

Answer: The & operator performs an element-wise logical AND operation across the two boolean vectors (students$passed == TRUE and students$age > 19), evaluating row-by-row to produce a single combined boolean vector of TRUE/FALSE values that dictates which rows to keep.

What would change if you used | (OR) instead of & (AND)?

Answer: If you used | (OR), the filter would return any student who either passed or is older than 19 (or both), resulting in a broader set of matching rows.

Question #5: Run summary() on students. Notice that the numeric column (age) and the logical column (passed) are summarized very differently from the character column (name). Describe what kind of summary R produces for each of the three data types, and explain why a “mean” wouldn’t make sense for the name column.

Answer: In terms of Numeric (age) gives statistical measures including the minimum, 1st quartile, median, mean, 3rd quartile and max. While, logical (passed) has the frequency table output, counting the occurrences of TRUE, FALSE and any missing values or NA. And for the character (name), it reports basic metadata such as the total length, class type and storage mode rather than mathematical calculations. The reason why mean wouldn't make sense for the name column, since it requires numerical values to compute an arithmetic average and character strings represents text data. So, a mathematical operations cannot be performed on them. 

Question #6: str() and summary() both describe a data frame, but they show different information.
Based on what you observed, when would str() be more useful to you than summary(), and vice versa?

Answer: I would use str() when I want to check the structure, data types just like text or numbers, and preview the first few values of the columns. While, I use summary() when I want to quickly see statistical numbers, like minimum, maximum, and mean, or count values to analyze my data.

## Part D — Data Frame Operations

```{r}
# TODO: Add a new column called year_level to students with values:
# 2, 3, 1, 4, 2  (one per student, in the same order as the rows)

students$year_level <- c(2, 3, 1, 4, 2)
print(students)
```
```{r}
# TODO: Remove the "passed" column from students by setting it to NULL
# students$passed <- NULL

students$passed <- NULL
print(students)
```

```{r}
# TODO: Sort students by age in ascending order using order()
# Hint: students[order(students$age), ]

students_sorted_asc <- students[order(students$age), ]
print(students_sorted_asc)
```

```{r}
# TODO: Sort students by age in DESCENDING order
# Hint: use order(students$age, decreasing = TRUE), or order(-students$age)

students_sorted_desc <- students[order(students$age, decreasing = TRUE), ]
print(students_sorted_desc)
```

Question #7: After removing the passed column, could you still run the filter from df-logical-filter (students$passed == TRUE)?
Explain what happens and why keeping track of a data frame’s current structure matters as you apply a sequence of operations to it.

Answer: No, running the filter will fail with an error because the removed column no longer exists. This shows why keeping track of our data frame's changing structure is essential during data manipulation, ensuring the code references active variable and avoids runtime crashes.

Question #8: order() does not sort the data frame directly — it returns a vector of row positions.
Explain, step by step, how students[order(students$age), ] uses that position vector to reorder the whole data frame (all columns, not just age).

Answer: Firstly, order(students$age) would analyze the age column and retuns a numeric vector of the row indices sorted by age, like 3, 1, 5, 2, 4. Then, the outer subsetting brackets [,] take that integer position vector and apply it to the row coordinate of the data frame. Last,  because we leave the column position blank, R pulls all columns for every row, rearranging the entire data frame row-by-row according to the sorted index sequence while keeping the data aligned across columns.

## Part E — Critical Thinking Challenge

```{r}
grades <- data.frame(
  name = c("Ana", "Ben", "Cid", "Dex", "Eli"),
  midterm = c(85, 78, 92, 88, 70),
  final = c(90, 82, 95, 84, 75)
)

# TODO: Add a new column "average" to grades that holds the mean of
# midterm and final for each student. Hint: (grades$midterm + grades$final) / 2

grades$average <- (grades$midterm + grades$final) / 2
```

```{r}
# TODO: Print only the rows of grades where remarks is "Failed",
# showing just the name and average columns.
# Hint: grades[grades$remarks == "Failed", c("name", "average")]
grades$remarks <- ifelse(grades$average >= 75, "Passed", "Failed")

print(grades[grades$remarks == "Failed", c("name", "average")])
```

Question #9: Suppose your instructor wants to know: “Which factor seems more responsible for a student’s final remark — a big drop between midterm and final, or a consistently low midterm score?”
Using only the tools from this lab (subsetting, new columns, sorting), describe — in plain language, code optional — the steps you would take with grades to start investigating that question.

Answer: To start the investigation, we would first add a new column  calculating the score drop between the midterm and final exams  (grades$midterm - grades$final), then use order() to sort the data frame by consistently low midterms and largest performance drops. Lastly, by filtering for students with low final remarks, we can easily compare whether those students struggled right from the start or suffered a major decline later on.

## Conclusion

A data frame is a table with rows and columns where each column can hold a different type of data like text or numbers, but every column must be the exact same length. Under the hood, it is basically a list of equal-sized vectors bundled together. It is R's go-to tool for real-world data because it works just like a spreadsheet or database table.
